\chapter{The Preterite --- Your First Past Tense}
\label{ch:preterite}
\hlchaptermodality{103}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the singular completed past of ser or ir and the known regular -ar verb hablar.}

Complete ES-C14-practice and distinguish fui/fuiste/fue from hablé/hablaste/habló using known words, context, and written stress.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ayer]{ayer — the word that opens the past}

\label{lesson:ES-C14-ayer}



\begin{quote}
Everything you have said so far happens now or later. This lesson gives you the one word that points the other way — backwards — and warns you what the verbs in this chapter are about to do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item voy a + infinitive — you can already point forwards; this points back.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a}, \texttt{vowel-e} — two syllables, stress on the last: \emph{a-YÉR} (\emph{ah-YEHR}). $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ayer} — \textquotedblleft{}yesterday.\textquotedblright{} It is two Latin words that fused:

\texttt{}\texttt{ ad    +   heri        $\to$   ayer (to)      (yesterday)      (yesterday) }\texttt{}

Latin \emph{heri} is the same ancient word as English \textbf{yester}day and German \emph{gestern}. The \emph{h-} fell silent and then fell away, the \emph{-ri} softened to a \emph{-y-} sound, and \emph{ad heri} — \textquotedblleft{}to yesterday\textquotedblright{} — packed down into one short word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Ayer} is a \textbf{time frame}: a word that tells the listener \emph{when}, before the verb ever gets a chance to. That matters more than it looks, because Spanish will not let a past time frame sit beside a present verb. Say \emph{ayer} and the verb must follow you backwards.

That is what the rest of this chapter is for. Spanish has \textbf{two} past tenses, and they split the past between them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{what it says} & \textbf{met in} \\
\midrule
\textbf{preterite} & it happened, and it finished & this chapter \\
\textbf{imperfect} & it was going on, or it used to happen & a later chapter \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English blurs this — \textquotedblleft{}I spoke\textquotedblright{} covers both. Spanish makes you choose, every time. You do not have to choose yet; you only need to know that the choice is coming, so the next few lessons do not look like arbitrary endings.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ayer} — stress the second syllable
  \item which of the two past tenses is for something finished?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two Latin words gave us \emph{ayer}? (\emph{Ad} and \emph{heri}.) English keeps \emph{heri} inside which word? (\textbf{Yester}day.) How many past tenses does Spanish have? (Two — one for finished, one for ongoing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fui]{fui — one past set shared by ser and ir}

\label{lesson:ES-C14-ser-ir-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You already use \textbf{ser} for identity and \textbf{ir} for going. Spanish now gives both verbs one completed-past set. This lesson keeps the same three singular persons you know: \textbf{fui, fuiste, fue}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three singular forms, two verbs}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{completed past of \textbf{ser} or \textbf{ir}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{fui} \\
tú & \textbf{fuiste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{fue} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{fui · fuiste · fue}. Each form can belong to either verb. The surrounding words decide which meaning is possible:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Fui a Madrid.} — “I went to Madrid.” The known \textbf{a} plus a destination points to \textbf{ir}.
  \item \textbf{Fue Roberto.} — “It was Roberto.” Identification points to \textbf{ser}.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Fui} and \textbf{fue} are one-syllable words, so standard Spanish spelling gives them no written accent. Plural forms wait until a later lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The shared set continues the Latin perfect family of “be,” including Latin \textbf{fuī}, “I have been.” Sound change and analogy reshaped the inherited forms. Spanish \textbf{ir} then came to share this past family with \textbf{ser}: a case of \textbf{suppletion}, where one verb draws forms from more than one historical root. English \textbf{go / went} uses the same broad strategy, although not the same words.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “fui, fuiste, fue”
  \item “Fui a Madrid.”
  \item “Fue Roberto — identification, so ser.”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three shared forms. (\emph{Fui, fuiste, fue.}) Which two verbs share them? (\emph{Ser} and \emph{ir}.) What decides the meaning? (Context.) What older family supplied the forms? (The Latin perfect family of “be.”) Next, reuse the known verb \textbf{hablar} to build a regular singular past.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hablé]{hablé — a regular singular past from a known verb}

\label{lesson:ES-C14-hablar-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{hablar} and its present singular \textbf{hablo, hablas, habla}. To say that the speaking was completed, keep \textbf{habl-} and learn three new endings: \textbf{hablé, hablaste, habló}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: present beside completed past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{hablo} & \textbf{hablé} \\
tú & \textbf{hablas} & \textbf{hablaste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{habla} & \textbf{habló} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{hablé · hablaste · habló}. This is a complete singular pattern, not a preview of plural forms. Notice the exact changes:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hablo $\to$ hablé} changes the final vowel and moves stress to the end.
  \item \textbf{hablas $\to$ hablaste} adds the past ending \textbf{-aste}.
  \item \textbf{habla $\to$ habló} changes the final vowel and moves stress to the end.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two accents, one natural stress pattern}]
The written accents in \textbf{hablé} and \textbf{habló} show final stress. Without those marks, words ending in a vowel normally stress the next-to-last syllable. \textbf{Hablaste} already follows that ordinary pattern — \textbf{blas} is next to last — so it needs no written accent. The mark records the stress; it is not the only change that makes a form past.

Now reuse known words:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Hablé español.} — “I spoke Spanish.”
  \item \textbf{¿Hablaste español?} — “Did you speak Spanish?”
  \item \textbf{Habló español.} — “He, she, or you-formal spoke Spanish.”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The regular \textbf{-ar} past continues material from the Latin first-conjugation perfect, visible in forms such as \textbf{amāvī, amāvistī, amāvit}. Centuries of sound change and analogy produced the Spanish family \textbf{-é, -aste, -ó}. The history explains a family resemblance; it is not one tidy letter-by-letter erosion for every modern ending.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hablé, hablaste, habló”
  \item “Hablo español. Hablé español.”
  \item “hablé and habló carry written accents; hablaste does not”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned past forms. (\emph{Hablé, hablaste, habló.}) Which two carry written accents, and why? (\emph{Hablé} and \emph{habló}; the marks show final stress.) What older family lies behind the endings? (The Latin first-conjugation perfect.) Next: choose between the two past patterns using only known words.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — two singular ways to talk about a completed past}

\label{lesson:ES-C14-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve the shared singular set and the regular \textbf{hablar} set, then use context and spelling to keep them apart.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete frame for this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item shared past of \textbf{ser} and \textbf{ir}: \textbf{fui · fuiste · fue}.
  \item regular past of \textbf{hablar}: \textbf{hablé · hablaste · habló}.
  \item context: \textbf{Fui a Madrid} expresses \textbf{ir}; \textbf{Fue Roberto} expresses \textbf{ser}.
  \item time contrast: \textbf{Hablo español} is present; \textbf{Hablé español} is completed past.
  \item spelling: \textbf{hablé} and \textbf{habló} show final stress with a written accent; \textbf{hablaste} needs none.
\end{itemize}

Plural persons, additional past-tense verb classes, new time words, and new place or person vocabulary wait for later lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The \textbf{fui} family continues Latin perfect “be” material and became shared by \textbf{ser} and \textbf{ir}. The regular \textbf{-ar} endings continue Latin first-conjugation perfect material, reshaped by sound change and analogy.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “fui, fuiste, fue”
  \item “hablé, hablaste, habló”
  \item “Fui a Madrid. Fue Roberto.”
  \item “Hablo español. Hablé español.”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give both singular sets. (\emph{Fui, fuiste, fue; hablé, hablaste, habló.}) How does context separate \textbf{ser} from \textbf{ir}? (A destination points to going; identification points to being.) Which regular forms carry written accents? (\emph{Hablé} and \emph{habló}.) The next chapter can add another past family without borrowing plural forms or unseen vocabulary from this checkpoint.
\end{tcolorbox}
